KEY MESSAGE 1...Rainy conditions develop tonight, tapering off 
to drizzle or intermittent light rain and onshore flow 
overnight. Cooler than normal temps Friday with best chances for
steady rain in eastern MA. 

Weak wave of low pressure over the central Alleghany Mtns is 
bringing a large shield of steady light rains across central and 
southern/southeast NY as of early this afternoon. Meanwhile in a 
narrow warm/moist sector, deeper convection was beginning to develop 
as of early this afternoon over the Delmarva Peninsula region. This 
wave of low pressure will bring increased cloud cover this 
afternoon, with light rains breaking out in western MA/CT around the 
PM commute period, and into the 6-8 PM window for central and 
eastern MA and RI. These rains should persist into the late evening 
before moving offshore early overnight. Winds then turn 
onshore/northeasterly overnight tonight as low pressure circulates 
over the southern offshore waters, which would support a scenario 
indicated by a loose model consensus of a low-cloud-overcast and 
either very light rain or even drizzle, with the better chances for 
this being across central MA, eastern CT to the eastern/southern 
coast. Pretty sharp gradient in QPF amts thru 12z Friday, ranging 
from less than a quarter-inch along the Route 2 corridor southward 
to about the Mass Pike, but then ramp up substantially to around a 
half/three-quarters of an inch for CT and most of RI and southeast 
MA. Lows mainly in the 60s given the increasing moisture. 

Friday's forecast is less than straightforward, with a larger than 
usual degree of uncertainty at this time range. This stems from how 
the low pressure mentioned above is affected by the deeper 
convection now getting going in the Delmarva area. Something of a 
loose majority of models keep a lingering/stalled frontal boundary 
with weak low pressure meandering near Cape Cod Friday, pulling 
northward late in the day into the evening. Official forecast 
follows that idea ... which keeps a lot of overcast skies around 
central and eastern sections of Southern New England, and the 
onshore flow and limited opportunity for diurnal heating forcing 
temperatures on the cool side of guidance, maybe a couple degrees 
higher than nighttime lows in the upper 60s to lower 70s. There's 
some opportunity for breaks in the clouds and relatively drier
conditions in western New England and temps reaching the 
mid/upper 70s there. Couldn't rule out rain at virtually any 
time in that solution, but the area that looks more poised for a
washout Friday is southeast and eastern MA. What we view as an 
outlier outcome is the 12z NAM and its 4-km variant, which seems
to struggle with a convective feedback problem, in closing off 
the weak low near Long Island and then very slowly meanders it 
northward. This leads to a slug of enhanced heavy rainfall 
totals over RI and southeast MA, amounts which could lead to 
localized flooding if taken verbatim. It seems like a spurious 
solution though as its 06z runs were closer to the above loose 
consensus the official forecast will follow; later shifts will 
need to monitor this for changes, but currently view it as not 
very likely to pan out. All told, have an additional tenth of an
inch for most of eastern MA and RI, but upwards of a half-inch 
of rain for the Cape and Islands. Friday night should feature 
increasing rain chances again though, ahead of the next wave of
rain for the weekend.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A wet and unusually cool weekend on tap. 

Bottom line up front: this weekend will feature cool, cloudy, and 
periodically wet conditions. The large scale pattern will be driven 
by an increasingly amplified mid level trough and cyclonic flow 
overhead. Sitting downstream of the trough axis through most of the 
weekend southern New England will be in the cross hairs of quite the 
anomalous plume of subtropical moisture; PWATs surge to 2+ inches or 
2-3 SD above normal for late August. Temperatures will be cool for 
this time of year as cool northeast flow takes hold at the surface; 
expect high temperatures each day in the low 70s (inland) to upper 
60s for parts of the eastern shoreline. This results in limited 
instability and majority of the rain will be stratiform in nature. 
However, dewpoints in the upper 60s to low 70s will lead to several 
hundred J/kg of CAPE so some isolated embedded thunder is possible. 
Otherwise forcing is plentiful with several embedded shortwaves 
rounding the base of the trough, favorable placement beneath the RRQ 
of a 300mb jet, and the surface low and associated frontal 
boundaries slowly moving overhead. Overall, while it won't be 
raining all weekend everywhere, rain showers will continue off-and-
on until the cold front ushers in a drier airmass Sunday 
night/Monday morning. When all is said and done the combination of 
rich tropical moisture and good dynamics will lead to rainfall
